items.title: Evenepoel Hoping for Better at Euro Champs: ‘I Wouldn’t Say I’m Out for Revenge’
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Belgian star Remco Evenepoel aiming to bounce back from what was a difficult, confidence-shaking world championship ride
items.lbText:
Remco Evenepoel in action during the elite men's Road Race race at the cycling World Championships (Photo: Jasper Jacobs/Belga Mag via AFP) (Photo: JASPER JACOBS)

Second to Tadej Pogačar last year, Remco Evenepoel has one goal in mind for Sunday’s European championships : to win.

The Belgian has already won many of the big one day races he has been targeting in the sport: he was road world champion in 2022, Olympic champion in 2024, has won TTs at the same level and has clocked up two editions of Liège-Bastogne-Liège and four of the Clasica San Sebastian.

He’s a winner, and Sunday’s mission is to triumph.

There’s a problem though: his performance last weekend in the road worlds.

Evenepoel had looked supreme in the time trial seven days earlier, and also dominated the GP Cycliste de Québec. But his form deserted him when it was most needed, with things simply not working out in the road worlds.

It is, he said, something that will spur him on.

“I wouldn’t say I’m out for revenge, but I was definitely a bit disappointed that I wasn’t at the appointment,” he stated, referring to what was one of the biggest goals of his this season.

“It’s definitely been in my head over the last few days.”

When both Evenepoel and Belgium teammate Wout van Aert failed to perform at their best level in Montréal rumors went around that they were sick. That presumption was furthered in part by the illnesses of Lore De Schepper, Fleur Moors and Lotte Claes of the Belgian team.

Evenepoel was quick to quash those suggestions in the pre-Europeans press conference held on Friday evening.

“No, no… Don’t start, hey,” he smiled when asked if he had a cold.

“I’m not sick,” he said, according to Sporza .

“Everything had gone well in the run-up to that road race, but in the end it was just a bad day in terms of feeling,” he continued.

“The intensity training in the days beforehand went well. But now I just have to switch the button and try to ride a better race on Sunday.”

Montréal was a bigger challenge for Evenepoel.

Although last year’s winner Tadej Pogačar was absent, strong riders like Paul Seixas, Isaac Del Toro, Mathieu van der Poel, Tom Pidcock and others were present.

Each of those riders will be absent from the European championships, as will US competitors such as Matteo Jorgenson and eventual winner Brandon McNulty.

The field is less stacked and that could work in his favor, provided the race is hard enough.

He’ll be keen to put the worlds disappointment behind him. He’ll also be spurred on by the thoughts of winning the European road race title for the first time.

“That’s a big motivation for me,” Evenepoel confirmed. “The urge to do it is certainly present. That was actually the case last year, but it didn’t work out then.”

The issue then was Pogačar, who dominated the race. But the Slovenian champion is absent this time around due to injury, which removes one major challenger.

Several of those other rivals from the worlds will also be missing, but there are still strong riders to contend with.

One big concern is the Italian Giulio Ciccone. “He is really in good shape and will definitely compete for the win,” he said. Primož Roglič is another. “He was good at Montreal and will be motivated for his own audience,’ he said, referring to the championships being held in Roglič’s native Slovenia.

What’s crucial is that Evenepoel performs at his best on Sunday.

He said the shift in time zones from Canada made things a little trickier and that he still felt the effect on Tuesday. However by Wednesday he said his usual rhythm had returned.

“The training has gone pretty well, so I hope everything goes in a positive line towards Sunday now,” he said.

If it does, he will certainly be right up there.

Canada didn’t work out well but Slovenia might.

items.title: Piganzoli Scoops Giro Dell’Emilia as McNulty Debuts Rainbow Jersey
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Matteo Jorgenson plays vital role once again in teammate's success, just one week after helping Brandon McNulty to win worlds.
items.lbText:
Davide Piganzoli (Visma-Lease a Bike) leads world champ Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates - XRG) during the Giro dell'Emilia 2026 (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images) (Photo: @DarioBelingheri/@GettyImages)

Davide Piganzoli ran out the surprise winner of the Giro dell’Emilia on Saturday, benefiting from the same dedicated teamwork from Matteo Jorgenson that Brandon McNulty enjoyed at last weekend’s world championships.

Just as he did for McNulty, Jorgenson proved the kingmaker for Visma-Lease a Bike teammate Piganzoli after he launched a perfectly-timed solo attack in the finale.

The Italian made his move on a downhill with 4.8km to go, quickly gaining time while Jorgenson sat on wheels and marked all attempts to chase.

He started the final ascent of the San Luca climb with a 41 second lead and gave it everything on the 2.1km ascent, with Tom Pidcock (Pinarello Q36.5 Pro Cycling), Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) and Ben Healy (EF Education EasyPost) all being marked by Jorgenson.

Pidcock leaped clear closer to the line and narrowed the gap to just two seconds, with Onley taking third. Jorgenson was fifth, 12 seconds back, while McNulty had a solid showing in his first outing in the rainbow jersey with tenth.

“I picked the right moment to attack, and it paid off,” Piganzoli said afterward. “We had several cards to play. We handled this race perfectly as a team. It means a lot to me to add this great race to my palmares.”

Although he won the recent Tour de Luxembourg, he looked far from the strongest on the penultimate ascent of the climb.

Jorgenson made his move there with 10.5km remaining, close to the summit, and went solo. Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost) brought back him before the top, with Onley also there, and on the descent they were joined by Pidcock and Piganzoli.

The latter made his move with 4.8km remaining, choosing the perfect moment. With Jorgenson blocking, he gained enough time to hold on until the end.

“I felt good in the closing kilometers, so I decided to go all in,” Piganzoli said. “I also wanted to put my teammates in a good position that way. We still had Ben behind us, who has a strong sprint.

“In the end, I was able to finish it off myself, but this was a victory for the entire team. I’m happy that I was able to show my good form from Luxembourg and the world championships here again.”

Saturday was the first chance for McNulty to show off his rainbow jersey and rainbow-adorned bike since his surprise win in last weekend’s world championships.

The steep gradients of the San Luca climb didn’t play to his strengths but he rode aggressively, going briefly clear with 19km to go and later remaining close to the lighter riders when they went all in with one lap to go. He ended up in the second chasing group on the road.

McNulty has made clear winning the worlds won’t prevent him from riding for team leader Tadej Pogačar and others, but he certainly performed strongly on Saturday. He eventually finished tenth, 45 seconds behind Piganzoli.

“Today was really special, racing in the rainbow jersey for the first time, and I enjoyed every moment of it,” he said afterwards.

“I gave everything last weekend at the world championships, so I knew I might still be missing a little bit today.

“It was a tough day out there, but there are still plenty of opportunities to come and I’m looking forward to the next races.”

McNulty is scheduled to ride the Coppa Agostoni on Sunday and then Tre Valli Varesine on Tuesday.

He is also expected to line out in Il Lombardia next Saturday, as is an in-form Jorgenson.

items.title: Dream Season Continues as New World Champ Vollering Defends European Title
items.author: sstokes
items.content: Demi Vollering is too strong once again, soloing to second consecutive European champs victory.
items.lbText:
Demi Vollering (Netherlands) wins the European road championships on October 03, 2026 in Sencur, Slovenia. (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski/Getty Images) (Photo: Szymon Gruchalski)

One week after becoming world champion for the first time, Demi Vollering has doubled up with the European champs jersey, successfully defending the title she won last year.

Vollering continued a dream season with an assertive solo performance, going clear on the final lap with worlds runner-up Kasia Niewiadoma (Poland) and her own Dutch teammate Puck Pieterse. They dropped the other favorites on the Možjanca climb, with Vollering then kicking clear alone with just under 15km remaining.

Niewiadoma chased hard but with Pieterse sitting on, the duo were 34 seconds back with 12.2km to go. They were joined by Elisa Longo Borghini (Italy) and Antonia Niedermaier (Germany), with Marlen Reusser (Switzerland) bridging soon afterwards.

That gave the chasers numerical advantage but Vollering was too powerful, driving onwards towards the finish and notching up yet another win in what is a stunning season.

“It is really a golden year,” she said. “It is sad it is already over. Only the TT, and then it is off season already. But I cannot wait to race next year all year in this jersey and hopefully have a good season again.”

Niewiadoma crashed towards the finish, losing any chance of a medal. Pieterse won the sprint for second, five seconds back, with Reusser and Longo Borghini third and fourth. Niedermaier was 15 seconds adrift while a disappointed Niewiadoma limped in 45 seconds behind.

She will rue losing the chance to go for a medal, but Vollering was clearly a class above everyone.

“I just really love winning and it never gets boring for me,” she said, making clear that she still has many dreams in the sport.

“I think also it is not only the winning for me, but just proving yourself and getting better every day. Working on yourself every day and seeing what is still possible for the future. I think that is what I love most about this job.”

The elite women’s road race had a very different course to that of last week’s world road championship. The course in Montréal was very draining but Saturday’s 130km event in Slovenia was primarily flat for the first two thirds. However, following the start of two finishing laps, things did get more difficult.

The riders would face the Možjanca climb on each of those laps and while it was just 2.1km in length, it averaged 10.4 percent.

The days break saw Carina Schrempf (Austria) and Margot Vanpachtenbeke (Belgium) go clear less than 10km from the start and remain out front until 39km to go. The first ascent of the climb saw Reusser surge with 35km to go and force a group clear containing the world champion Vollering, Pieterse, Longo Borghini, Niedermaier, Niewiadoma and Juliette Berthet (France).

However while these are all very powerful riders, the terrain enabled a large regrouping on and after the descent.

Franziska Koch (Germany) and Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig (Denmark) then played their hand with 28km remaining. They got 25 seconds but were gobbled up with 19km left, just before Liane Lippert (Germany) attacked on a ramp and was joined by Noemi Rüegg (Switzerland) and Femke De Vries (Netherlands).

That trio sped towards the climb with a lead of 20 seconds but were reeled in with 16km remaining. Vollering, Pieterse and Niewiadoma pushed forward on the uphill but when the world champion surged with just under 15km remaining, she quickly moved clear.

Niewiadoma chased, with Pieterse sitting on, and while Longo Borghini, Niedermaier and Reusser rejoined, that collective strength could do nothing against Vollering.

She was well able to hold them off, racing to her second major triumph in eight days.

items.title: ‘Larry! Larry!’: Fans Give Warbasse Royal Treatment in Historic USA Worlds Win
items.author: ahood
items.content: As Team USA’s road captain, Larry Warbasse helped others chase gold. Then Montréal’s fans gave him a moment he’ll never forget.
items.lbText:
Warbasse got a rousing reception in Montréal during the 2026 road worlds. (Photo: Andrej Ivanov / AFP)

Larry Warbasse had taken his pulls and was riding to the finish at the UCI Road World Championships when the fans started an impromptu homage to the popular American.

On the final laps of the world championships in Montréal, the U.S. road captain climbed through a crowd that tipped their collective hats to the 36-year-old.

Up the road, Brandon McNulty was racing toward the rainbow jersey.

Behind, Warbasse was getting a royal reception of his own for a job well done in America’s first elite men’s road title in 33 years .

“Yeah, even the last couple of laps I was dropped and I don’t know who started it, but they started just chanting like Larry! Larry!,” Warbasse told Velo . “Like the whole way up the climb, so that was pretty cool.”

McNulty’s Montréal worlds win was a collective effort for Team USA , and Warbasse played a special role during the race and behind the scenes.

As the designated road captain, he helped position and protect the American leaders until crunch time in the closing laps in the squad’s rainbow jersey-winning tactics .

“I thought with my experience and the years in the peloton, I could play a vital role,” he said. “I really wanted to race this worlds because I knew we’d have a super strong team.”

Warbasse had Montréal circled on his calendar ever since it was announced. It was the first North American worlds since Richmond in 2015.

He knew the Americans were assembling an unusually strong team, and he wanted to be there.

McNulty, Matteo Jorgenson, and Quinn Simmons would lead. Warbasse wanted to bring his experience to help them succeed.

“For me it was it was a huge honor just to even be there,” he said. “A lot of those guys have been racing together since they were juniors. I’m a little older but I know these guys from racing together and we had a really good vibe the whole week. It was just a group of American buddies.”

The unique bond helped McNulty and the team to pull of the miracle in Montréal.

A pro since 2012, Warbasse was the most experienced rider on the team of America’s golden generation .

“I was the road captain and my job was to make sure everyone was in the right position and be aware of the race situation,” Warbasse told Velo .

“Earlier in the race I was speaking with some of the other teams, trying to figure what’s going to happen. The race opened up pretty far out and I tried to stay there as long as possible.”

Warbasse said Montréal’s relentless succession of climbs and descents meant it wasn’t easy to stay together on the circuit.

Everyone had a solid game plan going into the finale, and despite racing without race radios, when the moves went down, everyone had a tactical blueprint to follow.

With the race going off ahead of him , Warbasse dug deep to stay in the race in case something happened.

And then something magical did start to happen. Fans spotted Warbasse and started calling out his name.

It’s a phenomenon that’s been growing the past few years, with fans cheering for riders like Wout Van Aert as they roll past. Warbasse is now part of that orbit.

Warbasse — who is set to race in 2027 with Tudor Pro Cycling — called it the coolest race he had done in North America.

“There were so many people on all the climbs. It was a wall of noise every time you went up each of the climbs,” he said. “It was pretty insane, a really, really nice atmosphere.”

Writing on Instagram, he said how much the impromptu love session meant to him.

“To all of the fans who somehow spread my name up and down every single climb on the route and chanted my name each time we went past, it felt like I was the one who won in the end,” Warbasse said. “I had goosebumps the whole way, and nearly had tears in my eyes feeling all the love.”

The fans also helped him follow what was happening up the road.

“All the people on the side of the road were giving me updates and when I came through, I could see on the jumbotron that Brandon was up the road,” Warbasse told Velo .

“Then once he won, everyone was going crazy. When I heard that he won, I was a bit speechless and I was just so excited.”

The celebration continued with dinner and a night out, a small gathering of teammates and a few friends. They celebrated the historical victory in one of the best worlds in recent years .

Back in Europe to close out the season with Tudor, Warbasse said he appreciated how rare it is for a rider to share a moment like that with his compatriots.

“Maybe that’s the only time in your life you get to be a part of such a huge victory,” he said. “I’ll definitely remember this one for a long time.”

items.title: Like Day and Night: the Two New World Champ Bikes Take Opposite Approaches to the Rainbow Stripes
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: We dove into the two new rainbow bikes from Colnago and Specialized, as well as a short look back at our favorite rainbow bikes of the past few years.
items.lbText:
It’s been just under a week since the 2026 UCI Road World Championships, and the paint shops at Colnago and Specialized have been hard at work.

To celebrate the two new elite world champions, Brandon McNulty and Demi Vollering, the champions’ bike sponsors have been hard at work to deliver them two unique liveries for the next year of racing. Interestingly, despite the two design teams working from the classic black, white, and rainbow color scheme, the two iconic brands have created dramatically different designs.

For McNulty, many fans will be excited to see that Colnago has gone beyond simply running it back with Tadej Pogačar’s design. McNulty’s Y1Rs has big, bold stripes on the front and rear of the bike, with a glossy black base. There are some other flourishes, but the oversized stripes steal the show.

Vollering, on the other hand, has gone much more minimalist. Her Specialized Tarmac SL9 is mostly white with clean accenting stripes of rainbows spread around the bike. Yet, the bike resembles Vollering herself, as it focuses on intentionality, and its flair is reserved for the fringes of the bike. Compared to McNulty’s Y1RS, Vollering’s Tarmac SL9 has a white base, with grey connective tissue.

We assembled the details of both of the bikes below, as well as a collection of some of our favorite rainbow bike liveries from the past few seasons.

To celebrate McNulty’s surprising Worlds win, Colnago has rewarded the American with a striking, bold rainbow design. The obvious showstopper is the amount of color on the frame. The design is anchored with a set of broad, clean rainbow stripes that cut horizontally across the bottom half of the bike. Like Pogačar’s Y1Rs, McNulty’s design has a black base rather than a white frame.

Beyond the bands, the black base itself has a few flourishes. Colnago coated the black base with a subtle glitter finish. That glitter doubles down on the glossiness of the look, while the brand says the effect is also a nod to the stars in the American flag as they glint in the sunshine. That kind of subtle extra detailing is also found in some of the other decals. The Colnago logo on the down tube, for instance, has an iridescent, holographic finish, adding to the shiny look of the frame.

Of course, Colnago is no stranger to outfitting a bike for the rainbow jersey. Pogačar, the winner in 2024 and 2025, had both a custom V5Rs and a Y1Rs. Nevertheless, in both cases it was a bit of a “less is more” approach, especially on his stripped-down lightweight Y1Rs we profiled at the Tour de France last year.

With McNulty, there wasn’t any subtlety—and why should there be!? If you look at the collection of custom bikes Colnago has made for Pogčar, they could fill several bike racks. For McNulty, this was the first. Boldness is imperative.

Compared to McNulty, Vollering has been striving for the rainbow bands for years. Her win was no surprise; it was the culmination of meticulous planning and tenacious riding that Vollering has leaned on for her career of success. Dutifully, Specialized has delivered a custom-painted Tarmac SL9 that fits that ethos.

“Winning world championships doesn’t just happen in one big moment; it’s thousands of small decisions leading up to it,” Emily Halwell, Concept Graphic Designer at Specialized, said. “This design celebrates that process. Riders spend years training, testing, and refining tiny gains, and the bike graphics reflect that. It’s a visualization of all those micro decisions building upon one another, ultimately leading to one goal: earning the rainbow stripes.”

Vollering’s design is mostly white with black Specialized details. The rainbow color was reserved for key areas of the frame, including the aptly named “win fin” on the back of the seat tube, the inside of the fork blades, and the top tube. Those rainbow colors on the frame, seat post, and fork are arranged in geometric patterns and lines that create an intricate design that can only be seen up close.

Throughout the frame, the design has a series of arrows, mathematical notation, and other notes that tie back to the Fastest to the Finish moniker, Specialized’s new central concept guiding its racing programs. The bike, in its small details, color flourishes, and design itself, is all about what the brand calls “the Equation of Speed.”

Even though the rainbow jersey was introduced in the 1920s, the rainbow bike is very much a 21st-century phenomenon. And, like so many of the fashion-adjacent cycling advances of the early 2000s, Mario Cipollini is at the center of it.

Cipollini only won Worlds once, but that was enough for him to change what it meant to wear the rainbow jerseys. The flamboyant Italian wore white shorts, rainbow bands everywhere, and had multiple Specialized bikes with big, bold rainbow decals. Love it or hate it, what is undeniable is how that look launched a new frontier for the rainbow jersey and everything that came with it.

Fast forward a decade, and cycling’s next master of panache, Peter Sagan, got three tries at the rainbow jersey and bike. Significantly, Sagan was a proponent of the bolder, black-based world championship bikes throughout his tenure in the rainbow jersey.

For many, the 2016 vintage of his rainbow Specialized Venge will bring back intense memories of envy. That bike can still be found in the annals of Facebook Marketplace, as the rainbow-bands-turned-camo will also loom large for a certain type of cycling fan.

One of the more underrated rainbow bike designs, and perhaps the one that is closest to McNulty’s design, is Mads Pedersen’s Trek Madone that followed his 2019 Worlds win. The bike was white, but was dominated by a broad, bold block of rainbow bands that cut diagonally along the front of the bike.

Perhaps it isn’t a coincidence that Pedersen’s unexpected 2019 victory is also the most recent example of a truly surprising result in the men’s world title.…

items.title: The Rapha Meltdown, Worlds Drama, and Selling $6,500 Wheels in 2026 | The Velo Podcast
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Inside the Rapha corporate fallout, Worlds drama, and balancing parenting with training. Plus: The appeal of a custom Firefly rim-brake bike, and how $6,500 Partington wheels can still compete against cheaper Chinese rivals.
items.lbText:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

You requested road bike content, so this week you’ve got it. Last weekend was Worlds and the race for the rainbow stripes. Logan Jones-Wilkins was in attendance, and Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, and I handed him the mic for a breakdown of what he saw. We talk about Brandon McNulty and whether his World Championship win was out of left field or expected. We also discuss Kate Courtney and a ridiculous positional rule that could have completely upended the women’s race.

Before that, we start with some listener questions. We received lots of corrections on the Canyon mounting system, but I argue that the technicalities are irrelevant to the greater point. The Q&A gives me a chance to put on my family-man hat and share advice for riders trying to balance their mileage with time for their kids, while Logan answers for his Haro bike.

Later in the episode, we dive into a couple of topics close to my heart. We start by discussing why the Rapha financial meltdown is a textbook example of a marketing fail, while Logan presents a strong argument for why the recent CEO departure might have actually been a voluntary exit after all. From there, we pivot to high-dollar bling. The new titanium Firefly rim brake bike makes no logical sense in 2026 but still commands attention, while the $5,500 Partington wheels serve as a positive case study on how Western brands can maintain appeal against cheaper Eastern competition.

items.title: Lachlan Morton’s Latest Challenge: Beat the Horses of the Old Pony Express
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: The Australian who calls California home will try to do the 1,900-mile mixed terrain route in just under eight days with a combination of three different types of bikes.
items.lbText:
Morton during his 'Alt Tour' last summer. (Photo: James Startt/VeloNews)

Lachlan Morton , in his undying quest to check off an extraordinary ultra-cycling side quest every year, has announced his newest challenge.

Morton will set out to retrace the Pony Express, a foundational route of America’s westward expansion, on October 5.

The Pony Express was the historic route used to deliver mail from the eastern metropolises to the early settlements and cities on the western frontier. Like the horseback riders who relayed mail across the plains, mountains, and forests of the 1,966-mile trek from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, Morton will travel light and fast.

Additionally, as those riders changed horses every 10 miles of riding, Morton will swap between his road, gravel, and mountain bike on a varied route that is built to resemble the historic route as closely as possible.

To raise the stakes, Morton will be racing the fastest recorded time set by mail carriers back when the Pony Express was in use in the mid 1800s.

“The way they could get mail across the country at that speed—before there was any railroad connecting it—was revolutionary,” Morton said in a press release. “The idea of people traversing such massive distances just captured my imagination, especially knowing a lot of that terrain.

“Think of these big open spaces—huge plains, mountain ranges—and you imagine a slow transition, but with the elevation and the vegetation it’s always evolving, and when you’re covering big distances you get a really diverse variety of riding. It’s a great canvas for adventure.

“It’s existed there for so long, and you feel like you’re participating in what the country is all about.”

The route will start in Missouri, take on the Great Plains of Kansas and Nebraska, before heading into the heart of the Rockies across Wyoming and Utah.

Perhaps the key of the journey, however, will be the long trek across Nevada—one of the most remote areas in the Lower 48—before Morton will finish through the Sierra Nevada, routes he knows well as he now lives in the foothills of California’s Gold Country.

While the route itself is not tied to any particular FKT or event, as his effort at the Tour Divide and Alt Tour were built from, his Pony Express effort will still have a time goal. Morton will be looking to beat the time set by the fastest Pony Express horseback relay.

In 1861, a team of riders and horses made the run from Missouri to California in just seven days and 17 hours to deliver Abraham Lincoln’s inaugural address to California to convince the state to remain a part of the Union as the Civil War loomed. That will be the mark Morton will hope to beat.

The Pony Express was replaced later in 1861 by the first national transcontinental telegraph line, but the mythos of the horseback mailmen lived on as iconography of the Old West. In his effort to take on the same route, Morton is hoping to understand more about what the true experience of the Old West was through the lens of his own riding.

“The appeal for me is the history of it,” he said. “It’s wild to get into that mindset—you’re a kid trying to make some money, and there’s this opportunity to ride a horse with a mochila full of mail through the night for 75 miles flat out, across remote, gnarly terrain that no one else has been crossing.

“It’s quite a courageous thing. It’s hard to imagine, and that’s why I want to go out there and try to get a better understanding of what that would have been like, and the difficulties they faced doing it over 150 years ago.”

Morton will be supported by his brother, filmmaker Gus Morton, who will be documenting the journey for a film and transporting the bikes that Lachlan won’t be riding over any given stretch.

Gus’ support will be limited, but with the remote nature of most of the course, when Lachlan swaps bikes, he will also restock supplies, just as the riders did on the old Pony Express a century and a half ago.

items.title: ‘That’s Ridiculous’: Team USA Captain Shoots Down Del Toro-McNulty Worlds Conspiracy
items.author: ahood
items.content: The controversy that won’t die: Warbasse and Creed tell Velo how Team USA’s bold tactics, not secret deals, put McNulty in the rainbow jersey.
items.lbText:
McNulty celebrates America's first world title in 33 years. (Photo: Tim de Waele/Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty had barely pulled on his rainbow jersey at the UCI Road World Championships before the internet goons started picking apart how he won it.

Tom Pidcock, perhaps frustrated at the finish line, threw the first barb, suggesting that Isaac del Toro helped his UAE teammate win the men’s road worlds in Montréal.

Then online sleuths found a clip of McNulty and Del Toro chatting at 36km to go, just a few kilometers before the Arizonan uncorked his winning move.

Team USA’s road captain laughed off the idea that Del Toro would throw away the world title to McNulty .

“No chance,” Warbasse told Velo . “I don’t think he was riding for Brandon. That’s just a bit ridiculous, obviously people are looking for storylines to build. To give it up? No way.”

In separate interviews with Velo , Warbasse and lead Team USA sports director Mike Creed picked apart cycling’s biggest viral conspiracy.

Creed countered that it was U.S. tactics that proved decisive, not some sort of deal hatched out on the road.

“It’s the tactic you learn when you’re juniors, use your teammates,” Creed said. “We’re just lucky we had three strong riders on really good days and we could do it.”

The UAE alliance theory just won’t die. Even nearly a week after the race, people are still debating it.

The final two laps of Sunday’s wild men’s worlds have been dissected more than the Zapruder film, with everyone seeing what they want to see about how McNulty stunned the favorites .

The fact that Team USA started with one of the strongest and most united teams in a worlds without the overwhelming favorite Tadej Pogačar doesn’t seem to matter.

“If Pogačar was there, everyone knew how the race would have gone,” Warbasse said in a telephone call with Velo . “We knew that if we wanted to get a result, we needed to try something a bit crazy.”

Del Toro, Paul Seixas with France, Mathieu van der Poel, and Belgium’s tandem of Wout van Aert and Remco Evenepoel were the big favorites.

The Americans were the ultimate underdogs.

Come crunch time, however, Team USA played their cards perfectly.

France had burned through its matches early, Del Toro was isolated and taking long pulls, and Belgium was all over the place. McNulty was waiting for his chance to pounce.

That famous video clip of McNulty and Del Toro chatting at 36km has became “magic bullet” for the supposed trade team alliance between the two UAE Emirates XRG teammates.

Warbasse just rolled his eyes when asked if he thought there was a pact in the making.

“I was chatting to my teammates also in the race, but that doesn’t mean that you’re working together,” Warbasse said. “If you’re next to your teammate, you’re probably like, damn, this is really hard, right?”

Creed made the same point , and nobody watching a clip knows what the two riders said.

“People do know that teammates will talk to each other during a race, right?” Creed told Velo . “Who knows what they said, maybe how hard the race is? He wasn’t about to give away the rainbow jersey.”

The awkward part of the theory is that it ignores everything Del Toro did trying to win the race himself.

Del Toro was racing like he wanted to win all day, even if the timing was a bit off sometimes.

But some point out the moment McNulty made his winning move with 32km to go, coming off the back of the group when Del Toro was at the front, and the Mexican didn’t immediately react.

Warbasse’s take is that Del Toro and Seixas took on too much responsibility too early, especially when Van der Poel went up the road with just over 90km to go.

And, like everyone else except the Americans, their legs were bien cuit going into the final decisive laps.

“I think both Del Toro and Seixas, they really assumed their roles of favorites, and they did a lot of work, probably a bit too much,” Warbasse said. “That really worked in our favor.”

With Quinn Simmons marking MVDP, their efforts played directly into American hands.

So when McNulty bolted, the favorites were already on their knees.

Velon posted a graphic on Instagram tracking the number of times the favorites accelerated over the final 100km.

Pidcock and Ben Healy topped the count with nine apiece, followed by Del Toro and Jorgenson with eight each. Van der Poel made six, while Giulio Ciccone and Seixas unloaded four each.

Jorgenson was covering moves. McNulty made one decisive acceleration that stuck.

Creed watched Del Toro taking repeated turns on the front. From his front-row seat in the lead U.S. team car, that hardly looked like a rider preparing to hand over a world title.

“I’m not going to go Alex Jones and put 90 clips online to make my case, but you don’t pull all day and then just give the race to McNulty,” Creed said. “If you just finished 270km and you’re frustrated, and your name is Tom Pidcock, that’s understandable.

“For everyone else, it’s just stirring the pot,” Creed said of the Del Toro-McNulty conspiracy. “I don’t know anyone who would give away the world championships.”

The Americans came into Montréal with three leaders: McNulty, Simmons, and Jorgenson, more than any squad in the elite men’s race.

That they finished with three in the top 10 — first, fourth, and eighth, respectively — shows how well the team raced.

“We were confident going in and we had probably one of the like strongest all-around teams, but maybe we just didn’t have that one like big name like a Remco or a Van der Poel,” Warbasse said.

Simmons circled Van der Poel as one to watch, so when the Dutchman attacked around 90km to go, Simmons was all over it.

With Simmons in front, McNulty and Jorgenson could sit on behind as their rivals did the work to pull back MVDP.

“So they were kind of able to get a free ride,” Warbasse said.

Creed described Simmons’ move as exactly what the Americans wanted. But getting a rider up the road only helps if he has the legs to stay there.…

items.title: Taylor Phinney Keeps Olympic Dream Alive with First Track Worlds in 16 Years
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Phinney, Kristen Faulkner, Ashlin Barry lead USA at UCI track world championships as Phinney chases fairytale Olympic comeback in LA.
items.lbText:
Taylor Phinney is heading back to track worlds (Photo: Tim Ireland/PA Images/ Getty Images)

Taylor Phinney , Kristen Faulkner , and Ashlin Barry headline Team USA’s selection for the track world championships in Shanghai this month.

The U.S. is sending a deep 17-rider roster to China as USA Cycling looks to build off of the back of unprecedented double-gold success at the recent road worlds in Montréal.

The 19-year-old Barry – who stampeded to solo victory at the U23 road race in Montréal last weekend – is joined by the 36-year-old Phinney in the seven-man endurance squad.

Faulkner leads the women’s team after she finished 21st in both the road race and TT in Montréal. The 33-year-old Olympic and PanAm track champion is joined by five more women on the U.S. endurance team.

USA Cycling is also sending four women to the sprint events after the team recorded a best-ever worlds finish last year in Santiago, Chile.

Phinney’s selection to the worlds team will stoke his dream of making a fairytale return to the Olympic Games.

The Coloradan came out of competitive retirement this spring with the sole mission of making it to L.A. 2028.

Phinney hasn’t raced track worlds since 2010, when he won the individual pursuit and hit the podium in the omnium. However, after winning gold in the U.S. national team pursuit this summer, it’s not out of the question that Phinney adds to a track worlds trophy collection that’s been gathering dust for 16 years.

The UCI track world championships run from October 14 through 18 in Shanghai, China.
