items.title: No Pogačar, All the Pressure: Evenepoel Riding For Redemption after Worlds Washout
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: 'Inexplicably bad': Evenepoel needs to reset the narrative Sunday at European championships as Vollering and Niewiadoma brace for titan battle in women's.
items.lbText:
No Tadej Pogačar, no Paul Seixas, no Tom Pidcock: The European championship road race should be a walk in the park for Remco Evenepoel on Sunday.

Anything less than victory would be a catastrophe.

That’s the message churning up the Belgian media as the bike-mad nation picks over the debris of what’s been treated as a sporting disaster.

After starting last Sunday’s world championship road race as the team to beat , the Belgians were bullied by Team USA’s powershow in Montréal.

Evenepoel in 12th, Wout van Aert in 28th.

There’s been a Belgian public inquest ever since.

“They all failed,” fumed Belgian pro-turned-pundit Jans Bakelants as he dissected his home team’s performance in HLN .

“I find it inexplicable that they were all so bad,” he raged.

Evenepoel faced an online flagellation after he admitted he “just wasn’t good enough” in Montréal.

The Belgian dailies are still debating roster selections and speculating over a team sickness after Sunday’s worlds washout.

Evenepoel’s historic fourth consecutive world time trial title and standout podium finish at the Tour de France were forgotten about.

Evenepoel can rapidly reset the narrative Sunday at Slovenia’s European championship road race.

He’s a tier above the rest of a start list weakened by fatigue, impoverished national federations, and straight-up apathy to a championship few seem to care about.

In fact, the one rider who does really care about this year’s Euros won’t even be racing.

Pogačar is a confirmed non-starter for his “home” race Sunday after this week’s “ will-he-won’t-he ” confab.

Meanwhile, Seixas is saving his legs for Il Lombardia, Pidcock’s British team chose to focus only on the TTs, and Mattias Skjelmose is out sick.

So who does Remco have to beat to reprise his curious new celebration and put the wheels back on his best season yet at the European championships?

Primož Roglič, Juan Ayuso, and Giulio Ciccone are Remco’s main rivals for the 196km race across Pogačar’s home turf.

Victory on Sunday would complete Evenepoel’s set of road titles, having already won the Olympic, world, and Belgian races. It would trampoline him toward an end-of-season showdown with Seixas and Isaac del Toro at Il Lombardia.

But even then, some might see it as a consolation prize.

The women’s European road race on Saturday should be a thriller that more than offsets any potential one-man show on Sunday.

Demi Vollering and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney will lock in for a third round of their battle royale in Saturday’s championships after they went 1-2 at both the Tour de France Femmes and road worlds.

Hot off a world title victory, Vollering is in prime position to defend her European title in Slovenia and earn a blue-and-white jersey she’ll never wear.

Niewiadoma proved in Montréal she won’t let Vollering have it easy.

Elisa Longo Borghini, Paula Blasi, Marlen Reusser, and Franziska Koch lead the opposition to the two women who have dominated this summer of cycling.

Both the men’s and women’s road races this weekend will be decided by the nasty ramps of the Mozjanca climb.

The women climb the 2.1km, 10% kicker twice in the back-half of their 130km race. The men take it on five times in their 196km race.

The women’s and men’s time trials take place on Wednesday, October 7.

Riders to watch: Vollering (Netherlands), Niewiadoma-Phinney (Poland), Longo-Borghini (Italy), Reusser (Switzerland), Blasi (Spain), Koch (Germany).

Riders to watch: Evenepoel (Belgium), Roglič (Slovenia), Ciccone, Pellizzari (both Italy), Ayuso (Spain), Pedersen (Denmark).

items.title: How Brandon McNulty’s Unconventional Training Plan Made Him a World Champion
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: High heat over altitude, and intensity over volume. Here are the details behind the training blocks that powered McNulty ahead of the world's best.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Zac Williams - Pool/Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty is a unique rider in more ways than one. Not only did he become the first American to win the elite road race at the 2026 UCI Road World Championships in more than 30 years, but he is also a rider who never goes to altitude camps. The Arizonan rides alongside Tadej Pogačar at the Tour de France, but instead of living on a mountain a month before the Tour, he is more often at home, training at 5:00 a.m. in the desert.

When McNulty lined up for the World Championships in Montreal, many considered him an outsider with a chance at a medal, but few thought that he had the capacity to win. The 28-year-old hadn’t won a race in the entire 2026 season, which was quite concerning after he rounded out the 2025 season by winning six races in two months, including the WorldTour-level Tour de Pologne and Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal.

Whatever happened in the 2025/2026 off-season remains a bit of a mystery, yet McNulty started the year with a few top-five finishes in February. After a DNF at Paris-Nice, McNulty was solid again in April before taking a short break pre-Tour de Suisse. The American showed good form while helping Pogačar, but he was still never in the top five throughout the entire race. His best finish at the Tour was fifth place on a breakaway stage, and the rest of his time in France was spent helping Pogačar.

McNulty’s results were nothing to write home about, so few considered him as a worlds favorite. But between his DNF on Stage 18 of the Tour de France on July 23 and winning the World Championships on September 27, something changed. This is how Brandon McNulty trained to win the rainbow jersey.

There were exactly 66 days between July 23 and September 27, which means that McNulty had nine and a half weeks to go from abandoning the Tour to winning worlds. First, he took 10 days off the bike. That is a long break in the middle of the season, but in hindsight, it was the perfect amount of time. McNulty then returned to training with five consecutive easy rides — that means Zone 1 and Zone 2, without intervals or any additional stress. He was riding 2-3 hours a day, not the 5-6 daily hours that you might expect from other professional cyclists.

His first workout post-Tour de France was a classic UAE Team Emirates session: four-minute torque intervals. We’ll see these a lot in McNulty’s training plan, and they are much harder than they look. In this post-Tour workout, McNulty did 7x4min at 45 rpm, getting up to a max heart rate of ~170 bpm at the end of each interval. Knowing McNulty’s heart rate zones and history, we can assume these intervals were done at threshold power, which is likely around 450w for McNulty.

Workout #1: 4-minute torque intervals (45 rpm) at 100% FTP

The day after this torque workout, McNulty completed 3x30min intervals with a heart rate of 155-165bpm during each 30min block. That means he was probably riding at Tempo, or Zone 3. McNulty said that he climbed the Voie Camillien-Houde in Zone 2 on the final lap of the World Championships, and by my calculations, McNulty’s Zone 2 is approximately 5.3w/kg, or 365w. That means these Tempo intervals are likely done at 380-400w, making for an interval session like this isn’t the toughest, but it’s crucial to get accustomed to riding at this pace for extended periods of time, especially when you are training to win races solo.

One of the key principles of McNulty’s training plan is progressive overload, and that’s exactly what we saw with his first ride five weeks out from worlds. The American did 3x35min Tempo at 145-155 bpm, up from 3x30min the week before. The same principle applies to the short torque intervals, which now added a 30-second sprint at the end of each interval. McNulty also completed an additional rep, which meant this week’s workout was 8x4min Torque intervals (45 rpm) at 100% FTP straight into a 30-second sprint.

After a few days of Zone 2 and recovery riding, McNulty went out for a two-hour endurance ride on Friday, but this one was different. Twenty minutes after he got home, McNulty was on the trainer for an hour with his heart rate rising from 130 bpm to 170 bpm by the end of the session. It’s extremely likely that this was a heat training session, something that McNulty and so many other pros have been utilizing before key races each season. The following day included the same style of Tempo intervals that we’ve already seen, but this time they were 40 minutes each.

The following day included a new workout in this block of training: 3x10min 30/30s from 160-170 bpm. Since McNulty is only hitting 90% of his max heart rate, my best guess is that these 30/30s are done just below and just above threshold. For McNulty, this could be something like: 30 seconds at 420w followed by 30 seconds at 470w.

Next up was another threshold interval session, but this time with much longer blocks. This workout was 2x20min over/unders with one minute VO2 Max followed by four minutes just under threshold. Intervals like these are designed to train your body to clear lactate, even at a high power output. The days of 2x20min at FTP are gone; almost every modern-day pro is doing over/unders instead.

At the end of this training week, McNulty did his worlds prep session: 6x4min VO2 Max and 6x30sec sprints. This is an incredibly hard workout, but one that McNulty uses to get into race shape. Not only are the VO2 Max intervals challenging, but the sheer number of efforts in this workout is a true challenge of fatigue resistance. Doing a fresh 30-second sprint is one thing; now try doing 30 seconds all-out after spending 24 minutes in your VO2 Max zone and sprinting five times full gas. These are the kinds of workouts that give McNulty the ability to attack four hours deep into a hard race.…

items.title: The Real Reason Every Cycling Site Publishes Reviews at the Exact Same Time
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: It looks like a massive media conspiracy when a new bike drops. Here is what is actually happening behind the scenes on launch day.
items.lbText:
Welcome to Dropped , a new weekly road and gravel cycling newsletter from Velo that brings you the latest ideas we’re debating endlessly on group rides, and a look behind the scenes of our coverage.

I recently saw a comment—I read all of them, by the way—asking why every cycling outlet posted about the latest Canyon Grail at the exact same time. It’s a common question, often followed by claims that we’re being paid. It brings up a fair point: why is there coordination when a new bike launches, and how does it work? There’s nothing nefarious, nobody is getting paid, and there’s a good reason for it. Let’s look at the Canyon Grail launch .

A month out, Canyon asked if I wanted to review the bike, providing only a launch date and time. I checked my schedule, decided the bike could be interesting, said yes, and sent over my size. Then things went quiet, and the bike didn’t arrive before the launch. It’s not entirely unusual for that to happen, but that’s why I didn’t have a launch-day review for you.

Instead, two days before the launch, I got a press release with specs and photos. That’s all I had, but it was well done with thorough information. I’ve also been doing this for a long time, and I bring plenty of banked up knowledge and experience. I read through the details, figured out how the bike fit into the broader market, and pulled out the nuances I suspected other outlets might miss but felt were important. I could have asked follow-up questions if needed, but the info I needed was there. I wrote the story and scheduled it for the embargo time.

You’ll notice everything revolves around that launch date and time. It’s called an embargo, and it’s the real answer to why everything looks so coordinated. An embargo simply means a media outlet agrees to hold its coverage until a specific time in exchange for receiving advanced information about a product. It might look a bit like a conspiracy, especially when every brand agrees to the same embargo, but it actually creates much better coverage for readers.

It allows bike brands to share information freely ahead of time so we get a chance to ask questions and genuinely understand a product. If I am able to get the bike ahead of launch, I get to ride it, take photos and video, and follow up on technical details. If there are no shipping or production hiccups, I have a fully tested, accurate review ready to go exactly when the embargo lifts.

Ultimately, embargoes prevent a race to the bottom. If they didn’t exist, the second I heard about a new product, I’d have to slam something onto the internet as fast as possible just to get people’s attention first. I wouldn’t have time to test anything or ask a single question. With an embargo in place, I can focus on the bike and make sure the story or review is actually worth your time.

Does knowing how this works behind the scenes change how you view launch day coverage? Hit reply and let me know if the coordination ever felt like a conspiracy to you.

All things being equal, the Canyon launch went pretty well. It wasn’t perfect, since I didn’t have the bike in time to publish a review for the launch, but I had the information I needed ahead of launch time. I’ll call that the middle ground.

A really great launch happens when there’s plenty of lead time. For the Pinarello X-Series launch earlier this year, I had exactly that. I traveled to Italy to see the headquarters and talk with Fausto Pinarello to get a sense of the company. I spent time riding the bike and had the people who designed it available for questions. If something didn’t make sense, the person who made the decision was right there with an answer.

Of course, I always have to remember that those people are inherently trying to sell a bike. They absolutely paint a rosy picture, and I have to lean on my knowledge to judge what reality is and what consumers will actually want to know. I always try to do this with an eye toward the ideal consumer: who does the company think this bike is for, and is it truly right for that person? When I’m at the headquarters with the designers, I have the resources to find that out and make that judgment.

When I left Italy, I had all the photo and video assets I needed, and was able to grab as much time as I needed with the bike. To me, that is the ideal scenario. Sometimes, I’ll get a bike sent to me and rely on video meetings with designers and lots of emails to understand it. That works too, and it can be nice not to travel.

On the other end of the spectrum, sometimes there is zero lead time. I haven’t heard from a brand, and I suddenly get an email exactly at the embargo time with a press release. I have to scramble to get an article up and hope the press release contains the details I need. Half the time it doesn’t and I find myself zooming in on website photos trying to spot things like a third bottle cage mount and waiting on the brand to answer questions. When that happens, the coverage is not as thorough.

I’ve already worked this into the article a bit so far, but what you have to understand is that everyone has the same information. What I try to do is look for the story inside of that information. Why does this matter to the reader?

I look for the unique selling proposition, then I tell that story. I typically like to share what the company storyline is—although not always unchallenged—and then react to that story. Sometimes I think a brand missed the best story of the product, sometimes I think the story makes sense and the people involved nailed it, and occasionally I think a product just does not work.…

items.title: Dial Your Diet for Training and Recovery: The Ultimate Guide from 52 Cycling Nutrition Experts
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Macronutrient targets, nutrition timing, supplements, and more: Everything cyclists need to know to optimize their diet for performance and health.
items.lbText:
Does your daily diet properly support your cycling training and recovery?

Are you getting enough carbs to sustain your biggest rides? But what about when you’re slaving at the 9-to-5?

What about protein – how much should cyclists really be getting?

And honestly, do you need that shelf of a dozen different supplements?

All these questions – and many more – have been answered by 52 of the world’s leading sport and nutrition scientists in a newly published “ Position Statement on Nutrition for Cycling .”

The weighty 18,000-word tome tells you everything you could possibly want to know about nutrition, on and off the bike.

It speaks to training, recovery, illness, female health, training at altitude … everything.

Big brains from WorldTour superteams, national federations, and research laboratories collaborated on the authorship. The UCI commissioned and rubber-stamped it.

There’s no bro science or social media “fact” here.

The paper is an epic encyclopedia of information for hard-training amateurs who balance biking ambitions with pesky real life. And we read every single word of it, so you don’t have to.

To give you the ultimate guide to dialing in your diet for training, recovery, and health.

What follows is based on information directly from the UCI bible, supported by Velo ‘s own research and calls with pro cycling team staff.

Note that we haven’t included on-bike nutrition or performance supplements here. Those are very deep rabbit holes that require separate exploration.

In the meantime, here are Velo’s guides on supplements and fueling .

And before we start: One important caveat.

There is no such thing as a “perfect” diet. Don’t get bogged down tracking calories and measuring skin folds. Use your health, happiness, and trends in blood markers, body mass, and power output as your guiding stars.

Take the below as guiding principles, not strict “rules.”

Overall intake and energy availability is the base of the nutritional pyramid. There’s no point finessing macro- and micro- nutrients if these are out of line.

The UCI paper recommends that daily energy availability should be 40 to 45 calories per kilo of fat-free mass, per day.

This calculation gives athletes a good ballpark figure for how many calories riders should eat every day, according to their training volume.

Don’t worry, basically nobody outside the sporting elite knows theirs either. We’ve laid out in the appendix below how you can calculate your own fat-free mass.

However, the UCI’s basic message regarding energy availability is that cyclists need to eat enough, all the time. Otherwise, all that training is a waste of time.

And trust us, you probably need significantly more food than you think. Run the numbers through the energy availability equation below, and you’ll be surprised.

1. The UCI paper is keen to enforce that lighter is not always better. That stance reflects how the WorldTour is increasingly focusing on power before weight in its quest to optimize the watts-per-kilo equation.

Amateurs should follow suit. Health and power output should be prioritized before any weight loss goals, unless medically advised.

2. Short periods of low energy availability (LEA) are “unlikely to be problematic” if the athlete allows full recovery time, and doesn’t fall into LEA regularly. However, prolonged LEA, or repeat bouts of short-term LEA, leaves athletes flirting with relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S).

Athletes need to pay particular attention to pre- and post-ride nutrition to safeguard against this damaging condition.

3. For female athletes: There are currently no generalized recommendations for how to alter dietary intake around hormonal fluctuations. The current consensus is that athletes track their cycles and adjust nutrition based on their personal experience and symptoms.

Carbohydrates must be the foundation of any athlete’s food plan. Forget the fad for Atkins and carnivore diets, and turn down the pre-pandemic hype for low-carb training.

Carbohydrates fuel the engine, support muscular repair, and play a crucial role in bone metabolism and immune function.

Carbs should be up- and down-scaled according to training.

Remember the saying “fuel for the work required”? Exactly.

The UCI provided useful daily carbohydrate targets for athletes at four activity levels.

We worked the recommendations through some example athletes to give you a quick guide.

1. The guidance above includes all the crap you eat on the bike. So, a 70kg rider who trained for more than four hours should include the glut of candies, gels, and café stop cookies in their recommended total of 560 grams of carbohydrate.

2. Carbohydrate targets look different for riders who are “carb loading” ahead of a big race or fondo. In those cases, athletes should eat 10 to 12g carbohydrate per day for two days before rollout. And this time, that’s on top of any carbs eaten in training on those days.

3. Prioritize carbohydrates in the immediate post-workout daze. Glycogen replenishment should be considered the first priority, with protein – contrary to popular belief – being second.

Target 1-1.2 grams of carbs per kilo of bodyweight within the first hour of training, and continue carbing at that rate for 3 to 4 hours thereafter.

4. The UCI’s panel of experts advises caution over “fasted” training. Training on empty should be applied strategically and sparingly, and shouldn’t be seen as a route toward body composition goals. Athletes should ensure full energy availability at the end of a day of lower-carb training.

Cyclists should eat protein like they’re bodybuilders . That is, they need a lot of it, spread relatively evenly throughout the day.

Protein supports repair and regrowth. Athletes can’t progress without it, whether they want to bench press 200 kilos or ride 200 miles of Kansan gravel. And for higher-volume riders, protein is crucial for protecting against muscle wastage.…

items.title: From the Velodrome to Space: US Track Champion Christina Birch Named NASA Mission Pilot
items.author: ahood
items.content: After swapping skinsuits for spacesuits, ex-track cyclist and Team USA member Christina Birch prepares for her first spaceflight with NASA in 2027.
items.lbText:
Former track cyclist turned astronaut Christina Birch has been named to NASA’s SpaceX Crew-14 mission. (Photo: Space-X/Getty Images)

Most retired cyclists settle for a new challenge like taking on gravel or becoming a TV commentator.

The former U.S. national team track cyclist and 11-time national champion has been named pilot of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-14 mission to the International Space Station, with launch scheduled spring 2027.

Birch, 39, will make her first spaceflight alongside commander Kayla Barron, Japan’s Makoto Suwa, and Russian cosmonaut Arutyun Kiviryan, NASA officials confirmed.

Their assignment involves “scientific investigations and technology demonstrations to help prepare humans for future exploration missions to the moon and Mars.”

That is quite a career move for someone whose previous office job called for steep banking, fixed gears, and an aerodynamic tuck on the boards.

Before swapping skinsuits for spacesuits, Birch won three World Cup medals and two Pan American Games gold medals across the team pursuit and Madison with Team USA .

She also made the U.S. Olympic long team for the 2021 Tokyo Games for the team pursuit squad that later won the bronze medal.

And cycling was already something of a career change for this overachiever.

Birch earned degrees in mathematics and biochemistry and molecular biophysics at the University of Arizona, then a doctorate in biological engineering at MIT.

She taught bioengineering before leaving to pursue elite track racing. She started racing on the track to cross-train for her initial passion in cyclocross.

And that was all before NASA selected her as an astronaut candidate in 2021.

In an Instagram post reflecting on astronaut training, Birch made some connections between cycling and her upcoming space adventure.

In cycling, she explained the sport generally rewards doing everything faster, while spaceflight means preparing to succeed when things go horribly wrong.

Her early training included survival camp in the woods of Alabama, underwater sessions to simulate space walks, and learning to fly jets, and she still found time to race the Leadville Trail 100 MTB race and run a marathon.

“Our goal, then, is to cross the finish line together, no matter the method or speed,” she wrote. “So we practice … and practice … and practice our contingency plans until we are sure that, even on our average days, we succeed in our mission.”

She recently served as a capsule communicator to crews during the Artemis II mission in 2026 in the first space mission to the moon since the 1970s.

Her favorite movie? Interstellar , of course.

Birch’s bike handling skills just might come in handy in orbit.

items.title: Bahrain Victorious Rider Alberto Bruttomesso Provisionally Suspended in Doping Case
items.author: ahood
items.content: Italian anti-doping authorities provisionally suspend the 22-year-old WorldTour rider, but do not reveal details about the case.
items.lbText:
Alberto Bruttomesso, shown here at the Deutschland Tour, has been suspended by Italian anti-doping authorities. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Bahrain Victorious rider Alberto Bruttomesso has been provisionally suspended by Italy’s National Anti-Doping Tribunal over alleged anti-doping rule violations.

The tribunal followed a request from the national anti-doping prosecutor to suspend the 22-year-old Italian, according to an update issued by NADO Italia on Wednesday.

Bahrain Victorious moved to sideline its rider during the alleged violation, and issued a statement Wednesday evening.

“Bahrain Victorious is aware of the provisional suspension concerning Alberto Bruttomesso following an anti-doping control conducted by NADO Italia,” a team note read.

“The team fully supports Alberto throughout the ongoing process and will cooperate fully with the relevant anti-doping authorities as the matter is investigated.

“While the case remains ongoing, Alberto will be suspended from all team activities pending a clear and definitive outcome from the relevant anti-doping authorities and the completion of the applicable testing and review procedures.

“Bahrain Victorious remains committed to the highest standards of integrity and to respecting the established anti-doping process. Until that process has concluded, the team will make no further comment.”

Officials said the suspension is provisional, but did not name a substance or provide any dates or details about the case.

NADO’s violation notice cited articles 2.1 and 2.2 of the WADA code, which cover the presence of a prohibited substance or its metabolites or markers in an athlete’s sample, and the use or attempted use of a prohibited substance or method.

There was no immediate comment from Bruttomesso.

Bruttomesso joined the WorldTour team in 2024 after racing for its development outfit, Cycling Team Friuli.

He won a stage of the 2022 under-23 Giro d’Italia and has recorded several top-five finishes since stepping up to Bahrain Victorious.

items.title: ‘I Know My Role’: Brandon McNulty Won the World Title but Will Still Fetch Water Bottles for Pogačar
items.author: ahood
items.content: Ex-pro Rasmussen questions a world champion shuttling bidons, but Brandon McNulty knows his role behind Tadej Pogačar at UAE won't change much with the rainbow jersey.
items.lbText:
McNulty knows he'll still be working for Pogačar in the rainbow jersey. (Photo: Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty might be carrying water bottles next season racing in the rainbow jersey, and he’s just fine with that.

Everything changed for McNulty when he won UCI road world championships Sunday in Montréal, but it won’t change his role of helping Tadej Pogačar .

“At the end of the day, Tadej’s still the best rider. So now it’ll be fun me riding the front of races for him in the jersey,” McNulty said after winning Sunday. “It will be really cool to race with him [Pogačar] for the first time.”

Back at his day job with UAE Emirates-XRG, the newly minted world champion knows he will still ride for the Slovenian superstar in his rainbow jersey season.

Whether everyone else can get used to seeing the rainbow jersey stuffed with water bottles is another matter.

Former pro Michael Rasmussen choked on his bidon at the prospect of a world champion returning to water bottle duty for UAE’s bigger names.

“It’s going to look incredibly uncool seeing him in the world championship jersey, sitting third-to-last in the UAE line-up with his pockets stuffed with water bottles, then peeling off just as the team’s two stars are about to race for the win,” he told Viaplay Sport News .

“If he’s lucky, he’ll be given a chance to see if he can win the Tour de Pologne in the world champion’s jersey. Otherwise, it’s going to be a bit bizarre.”

The scene of the world champion on domestique duties might be a shocker, but that shows just how deep UAE’s roster truly is.

McNulty and Team USA are still buzzing from Sunday’s historic ride to win America’s first elite men’s road world title in 33 years.

But the wheel quickly turns back to the pro team responsibilities.

McNulty’s world title keeps the rainbow jersey inside UAE after Pogačar’s victories in 2024 and 2025.

Everyone’s happy about that, especially team boss Mauro Gianetti, who was waiting at the line in Montréal to celebrate.

Wearing the prized tunic next season won’t reset the Arizonan’s place within the UAE’s hierarchy .

The world No. 1 missed Montréal after crashing out of the Vuelta a España and won’t race again this season . If he returns anywhere close to top Pogi-peak form in 2027, McNulty will again slot into the trusted helper role.

Yes, that means we might see the world champion pulling at the front or shuttling up water bottles.

McNulty is happy with the mixed role at UAE of helping Pogačar in the world’s biggest races and getting the occasional shot to win.

“I’ve been able to win some races in my career, but I’ve never been a superstar,” McNulty said Sunday. “It was more about having special moments to be part of races and be with Tadej winning monuments. I hope I made him proud.”

Even with the stripes, McNulty will also remain behind Isaac del Toro and João Almeida for grand tour leadership.

McNulty has yet to prove he can challenge for a grand tour podium, and his career best remains ninth overall in the 2025 Giro d’Italia , when he rode to support Del Toro’s second place.

UAE still hasn’t outlined how the title crown will impact his 2027 program, but Joxean Matxin Fernandez told Velo that McNulty’s remains invaluable among the team’s crowded roster.

“Brandon for me is a super, super rider and we believe a lot in him,” Matxin Fernandez told Velo during the Tour de France. “He is a super-class rider who combines the ability to climb and to time trial. For us he is both a super helper and a leader.”

McNulty might be back to helper duties, but he’s not a front-line rider who’s taking pulls on the flats or fetching water bottles all day.

He’s one of the peloton’s top “super domestiques” in the bunch, and UAE knows it.

McNulty joins the club of talented outsiders like Alessandro Ballan, Rui Costa, and Michał Kwiatkowski, who beat more heavily favored rivals to win the world title.

McNulty’s victory Sunday was his first win in 2026 because he had the legs, Team USA nailed its tactics , and the riders behind him couldn’t organize a chase strong enough to bring him back .

He won’t have to wait long to find out how racing in rainbow feels .

“To start with the jersey will be special. Hopefully, I can show with decent legs,” McNulty said of this weekend in Italy.

His Italian schedule opens Saturday at the Giro dell’Emilia, followed by Coppa Agostoni, Tre Valli Varesine, Gran Piemonte, Il Lombardia, and Giro del Veneto, UAE officials confirmed to Velo .

Then there’s the specter of the “rainbow curse.”

Every men’s world champion since 2006 has won at least one race in the stripes — Pogačar won 23 this season — so McNulty is hoping for some luck.

“Maybe next week in Il Lombardia or maybe a stage in the Tour de France next year in the jersey,” he told Sporza on Sunday. “If I could do that I would be satisfied with my career.”

That jack-of-all-trades role has been central to McNulty’s seven-year career at UAE.

He can empty the tank for Pogačar, like he did with an epic pull at Milan-San Remo , and then go for wins when the calendar opens up.

The stripes could strengthen his case for more opportunities, but UAE’s 2027 calendars still need to be worked out at the winter camps.

How much more McNulty wants the leadership spotlight also depends on him.

In fact, he signed a contract extension through 2030 with UAE to keep doing just that rather than seek leadership chances at other teams.

After leaving Montréal with the rainbow jersey, he might get a few more days with the team riding for him, but everyone knows Pogačar comes first.

items.title: Aero Testing the Factor ONE: 1,400 Miles With the Ultimate Aero Weapon
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: After two double centuries, a 1x drivetrain swap, and real-world aero testing, I know this bike inside and out. Here is why it's one of the best I've ever ridden.
items.lbText:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Modern progressive fit (if you want it) Unapologetic aero focus Exceptional momentum retention Straight line stability Stiff pedaling platform Distinct, aggressive aesthetic Stack adjustability without a saw

When the Factor One first hit the market, Velo did a short ride to understand the bike, and we wrote about what a departure it was from anything else on the market. What people see when they look at the Factor One is a wild aero bike, but for many, the real magic is the geometry. This was the first major road bike to introduce what is now considered modern progressive aero geometry.

Progressive aero geometry is a concept that solves the issue some riders have with getting ever more aero on a traditional bike. On something like a Tarmac SL9, most people can’t actually ride with no spacers because they don’t have the flexibility in their hamstrings and lower back. That means using spacers to raise the bars, which makes the position less aero.

To solve that, riders shove the saddle all the way forward and use a massive stem with short cranks. These changes rotate the rider’s position around the bottom bracket for a lower head and shoulders position in space without an extreme hip angle. Think of the body as a fixed triangle and rotate the front point down if that’s an easier visual. The problem with this arrangement is that you end up with unreasonably long stems, which impacts handling.

Progressive geometry solves this problem by designing the frame with this fit in mind. The frame is longer, the stem is shorter, and there’s a zero-setback seatpost available, plus shorter cranks specced. There are no odd handling artifacts because you aren’t stretching your weight way over the front wheel with a long stem.

That geometry concept is what Factor brought to the road bike world, but the ONE is still inherently a bonkers-looking bike designed to be the most aero in the world. I spent 1,400 miles, including two double centuries on two continents, testing what it is like to live with this bike. I didn’t just test it as it comes from Factor, though. I also wanted to see if I could make it even more aero—using scales and aero testing to check my work—and find out what that would be like to ride on those double centuries. Here’s what I found after a season with the Factor One.

Now that you understand the concept of progressive geometry and what the Factor One is designed to do, I will admit: that’s not how I set up the bike. Despite what you may have read, nothing is forcing you into using progressive geometry with this chassis. That is a choice, but the baseline design intent can still solve traditional fit problems.

For my setup, I actually put my fit in the hands of the people who designed the bike. I did not try to reinvent my position to solve a problem I wasn’t having. I already run most of my bikes with no spacers and ride 6 to 20 hours without issue. For the Factor, I went with the setback seatpost and the Size 1 bar/stem that is meant to mimic a 110mm stem on a traditional bike. Even understanding what that means can be a challenge, though.

Geometry charts don’t show the cockpit, and with the Factor One, that is an important part of the full picture. What I ended up with is a bike that is about 10mm longer from the saddle to the top of the hoods, while those hoods sit just a bit higher up in space than bikes like the Enve Melee V2 or the Specialized Tarmac SL9 equipped with 110mm stems. I’m a little farther out over the front wheel, and I’m running 170mm cranks—which are just a little shorter than my normal 172.5mm—but nothing feels drastically altered. I could potentially get my head a little lower if I fully embraced the progressive fit, but this specific setup solved a completely different problem for me.

The biggest challenge I tend to have with aero positions isn’t hip angle, but elbow angle. Often, I find myself a bit scrunched horizontally, which brings my elbows back beneath me. That acute bend puts more strain on my triceps and makes the aero position less sustainable over long distances. The Factor instead provides plenty of room for me to stretch my torso, meaning I am actually able to move from the tops down into the deep curve of the drops for long stretches. My forearms remain parallel to the ground, but I’m lower without being entirely reliant on my triceps to hold me there.

I love this not only for the comfort, but because it pulls my weight out over the front wheel with my head quite low—just like the designers imagined. It also enhances the signature handling characteristic of straight-line stability. The bike wants to go fast and straight, and this elongated position leans perfectly into that.

Like I said earlier, when you look at the Factor ONE, it’s not the geometry anyone thinks about. The bike is incredibly thin at the headtube, and every tube is wide but thin. The fork in particular is the most eye-catching. The legs themselves are as wide as possible when viewed from the side, but they also appear to be sitting at the “wrong” angle. It almost looks like a traditional bike and pushed the fork upright. There’s more to notice about the fork, but this pushed-back look is important.…

items.title: The Hottest Tech Trend in Pro Cycling? Shoe Laces.
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: In Montreal, we found that more and more pros are bringing back some traditional shoe technology.
items.lbText:
Around the start paddock at the 2026 UCI Road World Championships , they were everywhere: cutting-edge bike shoes with… laces.

While the vast majority of cycling shoes released in recent years use twistable Boa dials and other innovative quick-adjusting closure systems, a surprising number of the world’s best cyclists are turning back to tried-and-true laces instead.

Velo spotted Remco Evenepoel, Paul Seixas, Primož Roglič, and Matej Mohorič among the at least 18 riders in the elite men’s road race wearing lace-up shoes at the start line.

Why is this seemingly low-tech solution back in style? Specialized provides shoes to Evenepoel and Roglic, among many other athletes (who have the choice between Boa dial and lace enclosures), so we reached out to learn more about the decision-making process for pros.

“Riders are choosing laces based on a preference for the feeling of the closure and aerodynamic performance combined with lightweight,” a representative from Specialized said. “We know that comfort is critical and highly personal for all riders, and laces are one of many factors that go into selecting shoes for racing.

“While laces aren’t adjustable on the fly, some riders have the diligence to set them up how they like them, though it’s easier said than done. Most riders will benefit from adjustable shoes during long rides and racing, though choice is important to us.”

While fit is a big component, it is easy to read between the lines: if the fit works with either enclosure system, riders choose shoes for the aerodynamics.

The aero difference between protruding dials and low-profile laces is fairly intuitive, but the difference it makes is surprising. An aero expert who works in professional cycling, who didn’t want to be named due to the sensitivity of the data, told Velo that the benefit can be significant, ranging from 3 to 10 watts for switching from dials to laces in the same kind of shoe.

While we plan to do some follow-up testing ourselves with a combination of shoe configurations, Alex Dowsett has done wind tunnel testing on the comparison . Dowsett is a former WorldTour time trial specialist and current aerodynamic engineer for the XDS Astana team. In his testing, he measured a 1% difference, which translates to around a 4-watt delta in a hypothetical flat time trial effort.

In some cases, those gains are similar to what you could measure with shoe covers. In the past, we have seen the likes of Mathieu van der Poel use full aero overshoes for races. Those come with downsides of their own, including more time to put on the form-fitting covers, and the loss of breathability that makes them uncomfortable for warmer days and longer rides—like a 270-kilometer Worlds course.

We’re seeing shoe covers less now. At Worlds, even with cooler fall temperatures, there were about as many riders in shoe covers as in laces. Van der Poel eschewed both options this time, opting for aero socks and the new Shimano S-Phyre shoe with dials (Shimano doesn’t make road shoes with laces—for now at least).

For pro riders with lace-up shoes available to them, it seems that the mix of their lightweight upper and aero gains from their low profile has made them an appealing option. Couple those with aero socks, and you have a fast, breathable option.

While laces are in for the pros, it is interesting to see how different that is from the choices of consumers. On the other side of the fence here in Montreal, the overwhelming majority of riders have Boa dials, even if they have adopted aero tech elsewhere.

That makes a lot of sense. For most riders, the refined fit, high levels of adjustability, and easy serviceability outweigh a few watts saved in a time trial scenario.

Yet, if you care about aerodynamics, laces might be the biggest marginal gain you are missing.

items.title: Brandon McNulty’s Packed Fall Schedule Gives Plenty of Shots to Win in Rainbow Jersey Debut
items.author: ahood
items.content: After a wild worlds celebration, McNulty returns to racing this weekend in Italy hoping to ignore the pressure and do the rainbow jersey proud.
items.lbText:
McNulty will race for the first time since winning the world title. (Photo: Jean Catuffe/Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty is still coming down from the high of winning the UCI Road World Championships on Sunday.

After a wild night celebrating with Team USA riders and staff, it’s back to his day job with UAE Emirates-XRG .

McNulty will debut his freshly minted rainbow jersey at the Giro dell’Emilia on Saturday, then race an Italian autumn block that includes Il Lombardia on October 10.

The dream now is to win a race in the rainbow jersey.

“Maybe next week in Il Lombardia or maybe a stage in the Tour de France next year in the jersey,” he told Sporza on Sunday. “If I could do that I would be satisfied with my career.”

UAE officials confirmed his full calendar to Velo on Tuesday that includes a full block of one-day Italian races to close out his dream season.

McNulty will debut the rainbow jersey at the Giro dell’Emilia on October 3, then race the Coppa Agostoni, Tre Valli Varesine, Gran Piemonte, and Il Lombardia, the season’s final monument.

His Italian campaign continues at the Giro del Veneto on October 14 and the Veneto Classic on October 18.

His victory keeps the jersey inside the UAE team bus after 2024-25 world champ Tadej Pogačar missed Montréal following his season-ending crash at the Vuelta a España.

UAE brass were in Montréal to congratulate McNulty, though they may also have been expecting to celebrate Isaac del Toro .

The Mexican arrived as a five-star favorite, but McNulty and Team USA out-raced the stacked elite men’s field to take the first U.S. title since 1993.

McNulty got the royal treatment in Montréal, with a golf cart ride around the finish grounds and a standing ovation when he returned to the team hotel.

Team USA riders and staff celebrated with champagne, and someone posted a clandestine video of McNulty cutting up the dance floor.

Now, instead of heading home to Arizona, he’s flying back to Europe.

How much will the rainbow jersey change McNulty? The usually reserved and quiet rider is about to find out.

The Italian fall races are a big deal for UAE. With Pogačar injured, the team needs someone else to chase what would have been his sixth straight Il Lombardia title.

Yates is the defending champion at the Coppa Agostoni, while Del Toro lit up the Italian autumn last year, winning the Giro dell’Emilia, Gran Piemonte and Giro del Veneto and finishing fifth at Il Lombardia.

The Mexican, fifth after a hard-fought worlds on Sunday, has yet to confirm whether he’ll race the Italian block.

McNulty will now be at the center of attention when he returns to racing this weekend and will wear the prestigious rainbow tunic in road races until Sallanches, France, for the 2027 worlds.

The win Sunday will also move him up the hierarchy inside the already-crowded team bus at UAE, and with the world title comes some pressure.

He became the first rider since Óscar Freire in 1999 to take his first victory of the season at the world championships.

Every men’s road world champion since at least 2006 has won at least once in the rainbow jersey.

McNulty will want to ride the wave of emotion and momentum all the way to the end of the season.

After few nights celebrating history with family and friends, McNulty will get a few cracks at putting his first “W” on the board before the 2026 season ends.

items.title: Kasia Niewiadoma Signs with Lidl-Trek in Move That Will Reshape the Women’s Peloton
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: After second place at Tour de France and road worlds, Polish superstar steps away from Canyon-SRAM in quest to level with Demi Vollering.
items.lbText:
(Photo: NICOLAS TUCAT / AFP via Getty Images)

Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney will ride for Lidl-Trek from 2027.

The 32-year-old superstar and her incoming team confirmed a two-year deal Tuesday in a bombshell announcement that will tilt the landscape of the women’s peloton.

Niewiadoma-Phinney, a former winner of the Tour de France Femmes, has consistently proven she’s the best of the rest behind Demi Vollering .

The Polish attacker finished second behind Vollering this year at both the Tour de France Femmes and the recent road world championships. Their rich, long-running rivalry is one of the defining narratives of the modern sport.

After spending close to a decade at Canyon-SRAM, Niewiadoma-Phinney will bring Lidl-Trek a new talisman for the next two years.

Her GC and classics prowess will complement the squad’s current leaders Niamh Fisher-Black, Elisa Balsamo, and the prodigious Holmgren twins.

Beyond that, her arrival will boost the ambitious, cash-rich Lidl-Trek team into a bubbling “super team” battle that’s brewing at the top of the Women’s WorldTour. Vollering’s FDJ-Suez team and its challengers SD Worx-Protime and UAE ADQ have split into a separate echelon in recent years.

With Spanish super-talent Paula Blasi reportedly also leaving UAE for Movistar, the women’s peloton will race to a different beat next year.

Niewiadoma-Phinney acknowledged Tuesday she’s making a bold mid-career move in stepping away from Canyon-SRAM after nine years on its books.

“I am super excited about the next two years,” she said Tuesday.

“I have spent many years on the same team. The decision to move forward and change the environment wasn’t easy until I talked to Lidl-Trek. Instantly, I felt the team had a plan, trust and belief in me. I knew that when we joined forces we could aim for the highest dreams.

“I’m looking forward to working with people and professionals who have a fresh look at my abilities and at what we can achieve together, being guided from a different perspective and just new fresh air,” Niewiadoma-Phinney continued.

“I’m looking forward to learning from the team, what we can improve, how we can get faster and how we can raise our hands more often when crossing the finish line.”

No details were provided regarding Niewiadoma’s deal, but her palmarès will presumably push her pay toward the top end of the women’s peloton.

Vollering is thought to boast a seven-figure salary from FDJ-Suez that currently makes her the best-paid rider in the women’s peloton.

Lidl-Trek women’s team has also confirmed the signing of Arlenis Sierra, Ally Wollaston, and Julia Kopecký for 2027.

It’s a significant roster refresh, but one that’s dwarfed by what’s going on at the partnering men’s team.

Lidl-Trek men’s team has been on a huge WorldTour spending spree in recent months. Felix Gall, Jordan Jegat, and Jordi Meeus are the headliners of the seven names they’ve confirmed for the new season so far.

items.title: How Team USA’s Perfect Tactics Set Up Brandon McNulty for Road Worlds Stunner
items.author: ahood
items.content: Simmons marked the biggest moves. Jorgenson shut down the chase. McNulty finished the job in a Team USA tactical masterpiece at Montréal worlds.
items.lbText:
McNulty and Team USA stunned the favorites in Montréal with perfect tactics. (Photo: Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty ended a 33-year American drought by winning the elite men’s UCI Road World Championship , but this was an emphatic Team USA victory.

When McNulty blasted clear with 32km to go in Montréal, Team USA deployed perfect tactics as the sport’s biggest names tried in vain to stop him.

Quinn Simmons had already marked Mathieu van der Poel’s dangerous move. And when the favorites jumped to reel in McNulty, Matteo Jorgenson smothered the chase.

The Arizonan crossed the line alone , but his teammates had worked together all day to make sure it ended that way.

The eight Americans brought the legs and a plan to Montréal to put individual ambitions aside to deliver the stunning victory to make U.S. cycling history.

Here’s how Team USA pulled off the perfect team race at the Montréal Road Worlds.

To win, you need the muscle, and Team USA packed plenty in Montréal .

USA Cycling brought its strongest elite men’s team in years. No U.S. male had won the stripes since Lance Armstrong in 1993, and Montréal marked the best chance in decades .

Though other teams like France and Belgium saw more pre-race hype, the U.S. squad was quietly stacked.

McNulty, Jorgenson, and Simmons lined up as a rainbow jersey triple threat, three proven WorldTour winners with the legs to handle the grueling, classics-style course.

Backing them up were Larry Warbasse, Kevin Vermaerke, Riley Sheehan ( who substituted Nelson Powless ), Sean Quinn, and Artem Shmidt.

“I knew if we had the perfect day, I thought one of the guys could win, any of the three guys we had as leaders,” Warbasse told FloBikes . “It obviously was the perfect day.”

The mood was high as the Americans lined up with their maximum eight starters. They had numbers, depth, and more than one way to win.

And they started as outsiders as all the pressure and hype were on France, Belgium, Mexico and the Netherlands .

There was no designated leader, and with Tadej Pogačar out with injury , the team had a clear vision of how to race.

They decided the only way to win was to put aside personal ambitions and race as a unit.

“We made a plan [Saturday] night, we set our egos aside a little bit and we decided, okay, we just want an American to win this race,” Jorgenson told Eurosport .

Team USA missed an early break that pulled clear in the opening kilometers. It raised a few eyebrows, but the move contained none of the major favorites and was under control before the race blew up on the decisive Mount-Royal circuit.

“I spent a long time thinking about this, I wrote a little bit of a document last week when I was training in Vermont. I sent it to the guys with some analysis which usually my trade team does for us, but this time I did it myself,” the Idahoan said. “We made a great plan and like I said, we were able to set our egos aside which I think won us this race.”

The team protected their leaders from the wind and crashes on the fast, flat approach, and positioned them perfectly heading into the grueling and attritional finishing circuits.

The Americans were saving their firepower for the moves that mattered .

Crunch time came with about 90km to go, when Wout van Aert attacked and Mathieu van der Poel drove the move. It was the first major selection among the five-star favorites.

The 2019 junior world champion rode out of his skin to stay with Van der Poel. When the Dutchman accelerated again, and even when Van Aert was gapped, the Coloradan was still there.

His presence was decisive, because it meant McNulty and Jorgenson could sit behind, and force Mexico, France, and others to spend their energy chasing.

“When we had Quinn ahead, it allowed me and Matteo to follow,” McNulty said.

“I really think that we played the perfect race with Quinn able to follow that move with Wout and Van der Poel and neutralize it,” Jorgenson said. “Then Brandon and I were able to take advantage of Seixas and Del Toro, who spent a bunch of energy.”

Simmons was gapped briefly when the favorites started firing shots on the closing lap, but he chased back and finished fourth at the line, just missing a medal behind Van der Poel.

That was his best elite men’s worlds result, but his biggest contribution had come much earlier in the race.

As the leaders came together with just over two laps remaining, all three U.S. contenders were still in the front group. Team USA had the numbers it wanted.

McNulty was an ideal candidate . He thrives on long, hard efforts, and was hot off fourth in the time trial race.

After winning the 2025 GP Montréal alongside UAE teammate Tadej Pogačar , no one knew these roads better, even if the worlds used a slightly different circuit.

“As soon as it all came back together we could get one of us solo, which was the ultimate goal,” Jorgenson said.

McNulty — a quiet and reserved rider who prefers to let his legs do the talking — was at the back of a split containing Jorgenson along with Del Toro, Seixas, and a stack of favorites all lined out.

Then the Arizonan pounced off the last wheel, swung across the road, and poured everything into the pedals.

No one reacted immediately, and the favorites looked at each other behind him: You pull. No, you pull .

McNulty used his TT legs and knowledge of the course, and just kept going.

McNulty quickly pushed his advantage to just under a minute at the start of the bell lap, but the last trip up Voie Camillien-Houde climb nearly undid him .

The gap fell below 15 seconds, and the chasers could even see him near the top of the climb. Yet there was a pivotal moment of hesitation, and they did not or could not finish the job.

Whenever a major name counter-attacked, Jorgenson marked the wheel. The Visma-Lease a Bike star buried himself covering the endless surges.…

items.title: Updated: Tadej Pogačar Will Not Race European Championships Despite Late Pressure on Team
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: UAE Emirates-XRG quashes speculation of risky early comeback after Pogačar reportedly contacted his surgeon for clearance to race on Sunday.
items.lbText:
Tadej Pogačar is so desperate to race his “home” European championships in Ljubljana on Sunday that he’s putting pressure on his team to allow it.

At least, that’s according to reports from El País .

The Spanish paper reported Monday that Pogačar called the medic who operated on his busted collarbone four weeks ago in Barcelona. The Spanish paper wrote that the GOAT asked the surgeon Saturday for medical clearance to race the Euros this coming weekend, and was given the green light.

Pogačar is reportedly using that as backing for a conflict with his entourage at UAE Emirates-XRG, who are urging patience.

Pogačar broke his collarbone, a vertebra, and suffered a concussion when he crashed at 60kph last month at the Vuelta a España. It was a brutal fall that supposedly ended his season.

As Pogačar said at the time in a team statement, “This isn’t the way I wanted my season to finish. But right now, the most important thing is to recover properly and give my body the time it needs.”

If team brass buckles to Pogačar’s supposed wish to return, the 28-year-old will make a risky early comeback from his savage crash this very Sunday.

UAE Emirates-XRG told Velo on Tuesday morning that the reports out of Spanish media are “not true.”

Per El País , Pogačar has pulled a 180 from his previous acceptance that his season was over.

After missing the chance to defend his world title and being forced to watch his domestique Brandon McNulty win the rainbow bands, Pogačar is hungry to return to reimpose his rule over the peloton.

That’s contrary to his team’s ongoing reluctance to let him take any undue risk after such a hard crash.

But Pogačar has plenty of motivation to return to racing ASAP.

The European championships this weekend take place on his home soil. The course passes near his home town. He’s a national hero with home crowds to please. And he’s the defending European champion. His massive victory at last year’s race in the Ardéche is easily forgotten.

Pogačar’s home championship would be defizzed without him and his partner Urška Žigart , who’s also sidelined after she broke her jaw earlier this month.

Beyond that, the championship race against Remco Evenepoel (Paul Seixas confirmed he’s not starting) would serve as a test for Pogačar.

El País wrote he’s hungry to race Il Lombardia on October 10 to chase a record-breaking sixth victory in the falling leaves.

El País ’ reporting fuels a rumor that just keeps giving.

A mini storm of speculation blew up last week when Pogačar appeared on a provisional start list for Slovenia’s European champs.

At the time, UAE Emirates-XRG brushed it off.

“It’s probably an old list,” the team told Feltet . “Although he is back doing light indoor training, there are no plans for him to ride any more races this year.”

Since then, Pogačar has been bounding around looking chipper and race-ready.

He posted on Instagram on Saturday, sharing images from his first outdoor ride since La Vuelta , and his last day as world champion.

He looked fit and mobile as ever, and he’d not lost his sense of humor either.

The post includes a video of Pogačar comparing his fresh, palm-sized scar from collarbone surgery with his ride buddies, Eddie Dunbar and Zigart’s teammate, Gladys Verhulst-Wild.

UAE Emirates-XRG shut down the report from El País when Velo reached out for comment on Tuesday morning. “The article is not true,” wrote the team’s head of media.

Pogačar would be rolling the dice if he makes a comeback on Sunday.

He’s not a rider who shows up to roll around at the back of the bunch – he’ll be in his usual full superhero mode spraying attacks and railing descents.

El País reported that the surgeon told Pogačar on Saturday there’s no obstacle to him competing. But those healing fractures are presumably still fragile.

And while riders regularly return from broken collarbones within weeks, Pogačar would lose a valuable, rare opportunity to fully unplug and recharge for 2027 if he starts the hilly 196km champs.

He loves to race, and he’s got clear motivation to rush back to the bike and please his home crowds.

Or who knows? Maybe he just really dislikes his UAE Emirates-XRG trade team jersey.

He’ll be wearing it for the first time in two years next season if he doesn’t win the blue and white European top on Sunday.

items.title: Power Analysis: How Brandon McNulty Won Worlds
items.author: Will Tracy
items.content: The average effort in this tactical race doesn't tell the full picture.
items.lbText:
American Brandon McNulty celebrates after winning the elite men Road Race race (273,7 km) at the cycling World Championship, in Montreal, Canada, Sunday 27 September 2026. The UCI road world championships are taking place from 20 to 27 September, in Montreal, Canada. BELGA PHOTO JASPER JACOBS (Photo by JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga / AFP via Getty Images) (Photo: JASPER JACOBS / BELGA MAG / Belga / AFP via Getty Images)

When I wrote a preview article that named Brandon McNulty as one of the favorites for the UCI Road World Championships in Montreal, I didn’t think it was actually possible. Of course, McNulty was a previous winner of the GP Montreal, as well as a rider in form who had just finished fourth in the Worlds time trial. But he would have to beat the likes of Remco Evenepoel, Mathieu van der Poel, Wout van Aert, Isaac del Toro, Paul Seixas, and so many other riders. An American hadn’t won the World Championships since 1993, and McNulty hadn’t won a race in the entire 2026 season.

But when Team USA showed up with the strongest riders in the race, it was only a matter of time until one of those was soloing to victory. First, Quinn Simmons gave it a crack. Then, it was Matteo Jorgenson closing down key attacks. And finally, it was McNulty’s turn to go. The 28-year-old went solo with 32km to go, and held on to win by only 13 seconds ahead of Michael Matthews and Van der Poel.

This is how Brandon McNulty won the World Championships Road Race.

Before the start of the 2026 Road World Championships, there was a lot of talk about the course that resembled the Grand Prix Cycliste de Montréal. The World Championships used almost the exact same city circuits as the Canadian classic, including the Voie Camillien-Houde, a four-minute climb with an average gradient of 7.9%.

The GP Montreal included 16 laps of the city circuits and Voie Camillien-Houde, while the World Championships only included 12. Instead of additional laps, the Worlds RR added 100 kilometers of flat road to bring the total race distance to 273.4km. This makes a physiological analysis of the race a bit deceiving because the average effort of the race is not a true representation of what actually happened.

Quinn Simmons, for example, went on to finish 4th with an average power of 298w (NP 379w) for six hours and 17 minutes. However, Simmons only averaged 204w for the first 100km of the race, and 346w (NP 415w) for the last 173km. For the rest of this article, we are going to focus on the second part of the race — the hard part — once the peloton enters the Montreal city circuits. While the first 100km cannot be discounted, it’s unlikely that they added a significant amount of fatigue to any of the favorites’ legs.

The race truly began when Bruno Amirail went to the front of the peloton and started smashing the peloton to bits. Amirail averaged more than 400w for 90 minutes, with a Normalized Power of 440w on the hilly city circuit. He even pushed the lap button on his headunit, knowing he was about to do a 90-minute time trial.

In hindsight, Amirail did way too much way too early. What was the point of this massive pull? Amirail closed down the early breakaway, but that group never had a chance of making it to the finish anyway. The Frenchman didn’t set up an attack either. In fact, he rode so hard that the rest of the French team was fairly useless for the rest of the race. Their chosen leader, Paul Seixas, would cramp out of the chase group in the finale.

Amirail’s numbers are certainly impressive, but it’s the perfect example of wasting watts in a race that would reward tactics over pure strength.

Over the next two hours, there were countless attacks from the pre-race favorites, and soon there was a group that managed to slip away. With 80km to go, a leading group of six had formed that contained Van der Poel, Van Aert, and Simmons. This was about to be a turning point in the race, and just before the peloton hit the Voie Camillien-Houde, Pidcock was forced to chase back after a mishap.

Del Toro attacked halfway up the climb with Evenepoel, Seixas, and McNulty on his wheel. The Mexican kept pushing while Ben Healy and a handful of others were struggling to hold the wheel. Only 10 riders made it over the top of the climb on the wheel of Del Toro, who had just done the fastest ascent of the Voie Camillien-Houde in the entire race. Healy was one of the select few to make the split, and we can see that the Irishman pushed nearly 8w/kg for four minutes.

Healy – Voie Camillien-Houde with 78km to go

Following Del Toro’s attack, there was a lull in the chase group that allowed a number of riders to catch back on. Meanwhile, the lead group was split by an attack from Van der Poel, who was only followed by Simmons and Oscar Onley. If you’ve ever wondered what it takes to follow an attack from Mathieu van der Poel, look no further than Simmons’ power file: 880w for 26 seconds with a peak power of 1,093w.

Attacks continued to fly for the next hour, and this is when we saw the first cracks in the pre-race favorites. Evenepoel was getting dropped every few minutes, as well as Mauro Schmid, Van Aert, and Mads Pedersen. The Dane was so far behind that we didn’t even see him until the finale…he would go on to finish sixth.

With 36km to go, McNulty and Del Toro were chatting at the back of the chase group after the Mexican had just attacked. We don’t know what was said, but 6km later, McNulty attacked while Del Toro was on the front of the group. No one reacted, and the American quickly built a 30-second lead over the next few kilometers.

The key to understanding the rest of this race lies in the reality of fatigue resistance. For the final 32km of the World Championships, every rider went slower and slower. McNulty said he was pushing Zone 2 pace up the final climb, and we’ll look at those numbers in a minute. No one was setting power PRs on the final lap. In fact, most of them were crawling to the finish.…

items.title: McNulty’s Rainbow Jersey Was No Miracle—It Was a Decade in the Making for USA Cycling
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: Team USA's selfless victory for McNulty marks the arrival of American Cycling's golden generation on the world stage.
items.lbText:
When Brandon McNulty rolled across the line to win the 2026 UCI Road World Championships , it marked the end of a journey. Over the past decade, the United States men’s riders have been building momentum.

It started slowly at first, with promising results like McNulty winning bronze in the junior time trial at Richmond in 2015, and then accelerated with Quinn Simmons’ junior worlds road race title in 2019, Sepp Kuss winning the Vuelta a España in 2023 and Matteo Jorgenson taking back to back titles at Paris-Nice in 2024 and 2025.

Yet, the rainbow jersey that McNulty will take into 2027 is a whole different milestone. The U.S’s last men’s elite world championship was 33 years ago, when 21-year-old Lance Armstrong won in Oslo. The only other American man to wear the rainbow jersey before that was Greg LeMond.

“I’ve been in the USAC organization since I was 16 years old,” McNulty said after the race. “I was a child when I first met a lot of the people that are still involved in the organization. I’ve been to almost every World Championships since then.

“I was able to win the TT as a junior at the 2016 worlds, and then Quinn Simmons won the junior road race a few years later, so there’s been success. But I think the men’s road race has always been the dream for everyone in the organization. It’s super special to do with people that I’ve known since I was really a kid.”

McNulty is the leader of this generation that has elevated American cycling to near the top of the world rankings. While Sepp Kuss and Neilson Powless are both older and winners on the WorldTour level, McNulty was so talented as a junior that he became a model for what Americans could do starting at this younger level.

Both Kuss and Powless really found their success at cycling’s top level gradually as established professionals rather than from the jump as development projects. McNulty was different. At just 17, he was not only already racing in Europe, but he was also strong enough of a time trialist to set a course record at pro-level races in the United States—on junior gears. He was about as hyped as a junior cyclist could be.

It was during those junior years that the rest of the core of this generation also started to elevate their level. Matteo Jorgenson, who is a year younger than McNulty, is a key example of this.

When they raced in America, the two were rivals, as McNulty was the best rider on the Lux Cycling Team and Jorgenson was the top rider at Hot Tubes. Yet, in the summer, the two would come together for long European race blocks where they learned to race together as much as they competed against one another.

“I started racing with USA Cycling in Belgium when I was 16, just doing Kermesses for three weeks,” McNulty said of his time in the junior ranks. “At the time, it was a dream to be a pro, but you have no idea what that would have meant.

“I found success which, at the time, felt huge. Winning in Europe as an American felt crazy, so that confidence was the foundation. It’s special because Matteo [Jorgenson] was also on that trip. To know we’ve been doing this together for that long…it’s cool to grow up like that all together.”

That dynamic, the very friendly rivalry, started what effectively became a chain of talent. The mix of the US Junior National Team and the two dominant junior teams kept putting the most talented riders in scenarios of competition and collaboration. It was McNulty racing Jorgenson; then it was Jorgenson racing Sean Quinn, Kevin Vermaerke, and Riley Sheehan; and so on and so forth. That chain extends all the way to Ashlin Barry, who managed to do something that McNulty, Jorgenson, or Simmons couldn’t when he won America’s first U23 World Championship on Friday.

Altogether, it was that collective energy that built through the years that cemented the victory in Montreal. It was the interwoven story of those riders working to make the big junior teams, to beat out other juniors for the national team race blocks, and to work together to challenge European talent on their home turf. All of that set the table for the team performance that was remarkably cohesive for a national team performance.

“I think those guys were really lucky that in their junior and under-23 careers they got to be a part of those teams,” Michael Creed, the DS for the US team, told Velo about the power of the development structure that the US team created. “I run a devo team, so I know and appreciate what they do, because I know how hard it can be.”

According to Creed, that challenge—that grind—could have a direct relationship to the way they raced together when it mattered most.

“They raced like the US has won the world championship a lot of times, but maybe they raced that way because they knew how rare it was.”

Ultimately, the United States has always had riders capable of a top result in certain races. Before this generation, there was a strong cohort of riders like Tejay van Garderen, Ian Boswell, Ben King, and Taylor Phinney.

Yet, even with their success, having three Americans in the top 10 at Worlds, let alone winning the race, has never happened.

“There was a fundamental change in the psyche of American cyclists,” Boswell told Velo after the race. “My generation was very influenced by the previous generation. Almost every rider was a kind of GC type stage racer.

“That’s all what we wanted to be because that’s what we saw ahead of us. This generation hasn’t put themselves in that same box.”

For riders like Boswell, the inspiration was the likes of Lance Armstrong, Tyler Hamilton, and Levi Leipheimer. With that kind of legacy, and with the reckoning from the fallout of that generation’s doping hitting home after those riders already were well on their way to professional careers, that line of thinking makes sense.…

items.title: Did Isaac Del Toro Work For Brandon McNulty? Losing Rivals Call out UAE Team ‘Alliances’ at Road Worlds
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Team vs. country debate ignites after Montréal worlds as riders and pundits call out Mexico's Del Toro for 'helping' trade teammate McNulty.
items.lbText:
Tom Pidcock and Michael Matthews were left questioning if Brandon McNulty ’s “miracle” ride to victory at the Montréal road worlds was such a marvel, after all.

Speaking at the finish Sunday, Pidcock and Matthews both implied the American benefited from a cross-border alliance with his UAE Emirates-XRG trade teammate, Isaac del Toro.

The Mexican had been on the move all through the final two hours of the wild Montréal road race.

But when McNulty launched his audacious 32km raid for the rainbow jersey, Del Toro hesitated on the front of the group.

It was a moment that shaped the world championships.

The race then descended into a messy chase of half-committed riders spoiling their own, and their rivals’, chances.

Meanwhile, McNulty was left free to pedal squares – he admitted he was so gassed that he “could only manage zone two” – as he rode toward USA’s first elite men’s rainbow jersey in 33 years.

Pidcock was one of the few to go all-in on the pursuit in the final laps of Montréal, but ultimately finished seventh.

The Brit suggested after the race that McNulty didn’t only have USA’s Matteo Jorgenson and Quinn Simmons playing defense for him in the final loops around Montréal.

“It was hard to make the difference. To get the gap with the wind the way it was, with the USA team and with Matteo, he was super strong once Brandon attacked. And obviously Isaac is on the same team as well,” Pidcock told Cycling Pro Net .

“It was always going to be difficult to make a difference there after six hours,” Pidcock added.

Accusations of underhand trade vs national team alliances always come up at road worlds.

Tim Wellens even ruled himself out of riding for Belgium at Sunday’s race out of fear he’d either have to chase his UAE teammate Tadej Pogačar, or get slated for shirking his duties.

⚠️The breakaway has been caught ⚠️ Brandon McNulty 🇺🇸 launches a big attack and no one follows! 🔥 #Montréal2026 pic.twitter.com/8AoKQMh4eS

Pidcock dived headfirst into the team vs. country debate of this year’s race.

He was adamant the USA gained a State on Sunday: Mexico.

Del Toro and McNulty have raced together at the UAE super squad since 2024. They’ve teamed up to support Pogačar multiple times in recent years, including at the recent Tour de France.

They even shared leadership for UAE at the Canadian GPs, just weeks before the Montréal road worlds. They’re bike-riding bros.

“Del Toro was obviously working for McNulty in the end there,” Pidcock told Cyclingnews .

And Pidcock wasn’t the only one questioning Del Toro’s allegiances Sunday.

Belgian TV commentators kicked off when Del Toro and McNulty were seen chatting at the back of their group in the kilometers before the Arizonan made his decisive move.

Threads on X/Twitter , Bluesky , and Reddit have been filled with speculation in the time since.

They’re not rabbit holes we dare dive into, but there’s no question Del Toro had looked the strongest rider in the race up to the moment his legs left him when McNulty blasted up the road.

Spending 50km towing the chase group most likely burned out Del Toro’s motor.

Or, as some believe, the 22-year-old was metaphorically “bought out” by Team USA.

Matthews – who started the race as even more of a wildcard than McNulty – joined Pidcock in questioning what he saw in the chase group Sunday.

The Aussie didn’t directly call out Del Toro and McNulty, but the inference was there.

“There was a little bit of teamwork between certain riders,” Matthews told Sporza .

“They were riding a little bit together,” Matthews said Sunday. “If fewer teams had ridden together across national borders, then we would have caught him. It is what it is.”

Matthews won the sprint for silver in Montréal, 13 seconds back on McNulty. It marked a stunning comeback from months of injury and illness.

The ageless veteran might have been wondering if he could have achieved more in his 14th start at road worlds.

Whether Del Toro’s perceived reluctance to chase robbed him of a rainbow jersey is another matter.
